title: KVStore fragmentation mitigation & tiered memory pools proposal
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note proposes a pragmatic architecture to reduce long-term fragmentation and tail-costs in the in-memory key-value cache used by the serving runtime. The focus is on: (1) introducing tiered memory pools optimized for different allocation size shapes, (2) a compact-on-idle policy plus opportunistic compaction during eviction, and (3) lightweight instrumentation and guardrails to detect pathological fragmentation before it impacts SLOs.

Why we need this:
- Observed behavior: long-lived traffic patterns where many short-lived requests interleave with infrequent large sequence requests cause allocator churn and fragmentation. Over months this produces effective usable capacity loss and increased fallback to CPU/host swap-like slow-paths (higher latency, cost).
- Current mitigations (single allocator with slab buckets) work for steady-state mixes but are brittle when workloads shift (e.g., eval workloads with long context windows).
- We need an approach that preserves fast allocation for the common case, keeps memory utilization predictable for Dedicated customers, and provides cheap diagnostics and automatic recovery before operator intervention is required.

Design goals and constraints:
- Goal: keep effective fragmentation overhead < 6% for 95% of deployments and provide bounded degradation modes for the remaining 5%.
- Low-latency alloc/free path: hot path must be lock-free or use per-core arenas with minimal cross-core synchronization.
- Predictable memory accounting per-tenant/model: allow reservation/soft-limits to enforce capacity for Dedicated instances.
- Incremental rollout: must be togglable via runtime flags and safe to revert.
- Minimal change to model runtime loop and token path; compaction should be off the critical token emission path.

Proposal summary (high level):
1) Tiered pool layout
   - Tiny pool (<= 128 bytes): per-core freelists cached in thread-local structures; optimized for KV metadata and small control objects.
   - Small pool (129B - 8KB): slab allocators with fixed-size classes (powers-of-two-ish, but tuned empirically from real allocation histograms). Slabs are per-NUMA node with hot caches.
   - Medium pool (8KB - 1MB): chunked arenas that allocate contiguous ranges; chunks are used to hold frequently-referenced key-value entries with small fragmentation potential.
   - Large pool (>1MB): direct mmap/hugepages allocations handled by the OS path; entries here are rare (long contexts or large embeddings).
   - Each pool has a soft reserve and an eviction pressure headroom indicator we expose to the routing/quotas layer.

2) Compact-on-idle + opportunistic compaction
   - Background compactors per NUMA node that run when CPU idle or memory pressure threshold crossed. They perform: (a) in-place consolidation of partially filled slabs, (b) copying live entries out of fragmented chunks into new contiguous regions and freeing the old pages.
   - Compaction is rate-limited and preemptible; we track compaction work units and expose them to the scheduler to avoid clogging GPU-hosting machines during busy periods.
   - Opportunistic compaction during eviction: when eviction of an entry would free < X% of its hosting slab/chunk, the evictor can attempt a short-copy compaction (bounded by time/bytes) to batch a few adjacent evictions and reclaim a whole slab/chunk.

3) Promotion/demotion and cross-pool migration
   - Hot list: a per-core MRU list with lightweight sampling to keep frequently accessed small entries in tiny/small pools.
   - Cold demotion: entries that are not touched for a TTL window are candidates to be moved to a compacted cold-chunk area (dense packing) or spilled to a secondary store (if present) to free hot pool capacity.
   - Automatic promotion path for entries whose access frequency shifts up. Movement costs charged to the tenant for accounting and diagnostics.

4) Eviction policies and fragmentation-aware scoring
   - Base scoring = recency + size-weighted cost. Add fragmentation multiplier derived from slab/chunk fill-ratio. Evict candidates that, when removed, maximize reclaimed contiguous space rather than simply lowest recency.
   - Compact-first eviction mode: if the eviction candidate set contains many entries from one partially-filled slab, attempt a quick compact (<=2ms) and then evict whole slab(s) to reclaim sizable contiguous blocks.

5) Memory accounting and tenant reservations
   - Per-tenant soft reservations with hard enforcement in Dedicated mode. Soft reservations can exceed physical capacity in Hosted mode but will trigger routing fallbacks and autoscaling signals.
   - Track two forms of usage: logical (sum of KV value sizes) and resident (page-backed bytes). Fragmentation = resident - logical. Expose both via console with moving-window percentiles.

6) Fragmentation instrumentation and alerting
   - Minimal on-path instrumentation: sampling-based histograms for allocation sizes, per-pool fill ratios, slab/chunk reuse counters, compaction rate and reclaimed bytes, and per-tenant fragmentation ratios.
   - Proactive alerts: fragmentation ratio > 12% for 10m triggers a low-priority alert and a diagnostic snapshot (allocation histogram, top candidate keys, most-fragmented slabs/chunks). >20% triggers autoscaling fallback in Hosted and an emergency compaction in Dedicated.
   - Expose an API endpoint for a diagnostic dump (limited by RBAC) that includes a compact summary and an opt-in full heap walk for debugging.

7) Operational controls and runtime flags
   - Flags to toggle: tiered layout, compact-on-idle, opportunistic compaction, compact-first eviction, per-tenant reservations.
   - Config knobs: compaction rate limit (bytes/sec), compaction time budget per cycle (ms), slab sizes set, migration cost budget per tenant (bytes/second), fragmentation alert thresholds.

Implementation notes and rationale:
- Why tiered pools not a single slabless allocator? Tiering gives better isolation for very small control structures vs larger KV payloads; it reduces cross-size fragmentation and makes compaction scopes smaller and cheaper.
- Why compact-on-idle instead of constant background compaction? We want to avoid interfering with the critical inference path. Idle or pressure-triggered compaction still makes progress without hurting latency.
- Why bounded opportunistic compaction during eviction? Some fragmentation cases only manifest at eviction time; bounded compaction converts many small frees into reclaimable contiguous blocks.

Data migration and rollout plan:
- Phase 0 (canary): compile-time flag off by default. Deploy to internal dev cluster with synthetic fragmentation workloads and run eviction/compaction stress tests.
- Phase 1 (opt-in): enable in a subset of Dedicated customers who opt in. Collect telemetry for 7 days.
- Phase 2 (gradual rollout): enable for Hosted in low-traffic regions with compaction rate low. Monitor fragmentation, p99 latency, and compaction CPU.
- Rollback: disable compaction flags and allow normal eviction behavior; compaction-in-progress cancels and yields freed memory eventually. Have an operator-run emergency compaction path for urgent reclamation.

Testing and benchmark plan:
- Microbenchmarks: allocator-only tests with synthetic mix from real traces (use traces from SRV-alloc-hist-2025-08). Measure resident vs logical bytes, alloc/free latency, and compaction overhead.
- End-to-end: simulate mixed workloads (chat + long-horizon evals) on a multi-NUMA machine and detect fragmentation growth across days.
- Cost/benefit: for each test we measure reclaimed bytes per compaction-second and CPU cost; target > 100MB reclaimed per 100ms compaction work on average for medium workloads.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- Thresholds: what is the right size boundary between small and medium pools? Needs empirical tuning against allocation histograms from production.
- Migration cost accounting: should tenants be billed for promotion/demotion copy costs? That helps nudge workloads but adds billing complexity.
- Interaction with OS swapping: on some instance types we observed kernel-level page reclamation that interacts poorly with our compaction — need a pre-test matrix per instance family.
- Cold-spill policy: we propose optional spill-to-secondary-store in Private deployments; need to define API and latency expectations.

Next steps and action items:
- Instrumentation spike (owner: Liam) to pull realistic allocation histograms by pool and tenant. Due: 2025-09-12.
- Prototype compact-on-idle worker and run microbenchmarks (owner: Ayesha). Due: 2025-09-26.
- Add compaction/gc knobs to runtime flags and surface defaults in Dedicated config (owner: Marisol). Due: 2025-09-30.
- Create test harness for eviction+compaction scenarios and add to CI perf jobs (owner: Jon). Due: 2025-10-07.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a systems-first proposal intended to be conservative on the hot path. Expect iterative tuning. Please focus reviews on (a) expected allocation shapes we missed, (b) insufficient guardrails that could cause compaction to reduce p99 latency headroom, and (c) observable metrics we should expose for SRE.

Quick links and references:
- Relevant prior notes: SRV-alloc-hist-2025-08 (internal trace dump), kvstore-evict-sim-2025 (sim scripts).
- Related code: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/blob/main/allocator/arena.cc (see arena growth logic).

Unresolved: compaction heuristics and exact pool cutoffs (see Open questions).

-- End of proposal --
